phases: The Year That Will Not Settle
lesson.grammar_point: inversion after negative and restrictive adverbials

listenings.text: So, the archive. Four hundred and twelve boxes, opened over nineteen months, and most of it is exactly what you would expect: budgets, staffing, complaints about the heating. But three documents changed the shape of the thing. The most important is a memorandum from 1979, ten years before the events we are discussing, in which two departments are already arguing about precisely the question that would later be presented as sudden. Ten years. Now, why did the old account survive so long? Not because anybody was hiding anything. It survived because it was elegant, and because nobody had a particular reason to test it. That is usually the answer, and it is far less interesting than a conspiracy.

I want to be fair to this book, because the research is serious and nobody disputes the archive work. My objection is narrower than my colleagues' and, I think, harder to answer. The author treats one memorandum as decisive. Three other documents from the same eighteen months point the other way, and they are dealt with in a single footnote. Now, I am not accusing him of dishonesty. Nothing of the kind. I think he is simply too fond of his own finding, which is the most human failing there is in this profession. Read the book. Then read the footnote, and ask yourself why it is a footnote.

extra_audio.text: Ruth says her colleagues complained about the column without reading past the second paragraph. He tells her what struck him was the admission that the old version did not hold up to scrutiny. She explains that what they really object to is being told the old story was received wisdom. He agrees, but refuses to say the whole account was wrong, only that the tidiness was overstated. She asks what would change his mind, and he answers that only a date that does not fit would do it.

reading.rtitle: The Year That Refuses to Settle
paras: For about fifteen years the story of 1989 was told in one direction. The wall came down, the archives opened, and the ending seemed to be known while the events were still happening. It was received wisdom by 1995, and received wisdom is the most comfortable kind of belief there is: nobody has to defend it, because nobody is attacking it.

Then the archives themselves began to complicate it. Documents traced the decision back to arguments inside ministries that the public version had glossed over entirely — long-standing disputes, some of them a decade old, which had laid the groundwork years before anybody in the street had a reason to notice. A revisionist account appeared in 2004, and it was at odds with almost everything being taught in schools.

Not only did the new reading survive scrutiny, but it also held up better than the old one, which turned out to rest on three memoirs and a great deal of hindsight. That does not make the year a footnote. It was a watershed moment by any measure, and the upheaval that followed was real. What has been overstated is the tidiness of it — the sense that somebody set the stage and the actors simply walked on and said their lines.

This is what historians mean when they say that a subject has not settled. Rarely does a consensus collapse all at once. It comes to a head slowly, over a generation, as one detail after another casts doubt on the version everybody learned at school. And in thirty years the account we are reading now will look, in its turn, very much like a product of its time.
